Corporate websites are still too often evaluated using an outdated logic: as digital storefronts.

For B2B businesses, i.e. becoming insufficient.

If initial search, comparison, and supplier selection are gradually shifting to AI agents, the economic role of the website changes. What matters is no longer just presentation, but the quality of digital representation.

The key question shifts. Not how convincingly a page is designed, but which properties of the business can be machine-read and verified independently.

This matters for a simple reason: if an agent sees only price, lead time, and availability, the supplier enters product comparison faster. Actual qualification, work history, and the boundaries of responsibility remain invisible to the system.

This leads to a more mature architectural model: a single source of truth for both humans and agents, machine-readable operational facts, and a separate trust layer for material claims.

This is not about a fashionable add-on, but about digital infrastructure. Identity. Provenance. Accountability. Signed attestations where risk and obligations arise.

This is especially relevant in the DACH context. Regulatory constraints and data minimization can function not only as a cost, but also as a structural advantage in agent-based scenarios.

At the same time, this does not imply dependence on a single protocol or platform. Over the long term, resilience comes from owning your own business model and projecting it outward correctly.

The human layer also remains essential. It is needed where action becomes legally, financially, or operationally irreversible.

In this article, I examine this shift as a question of architecture and the economic viability of the digital layer.

Which part of your website today actually functions as representation rather than as a storefront?
